# Progress, Property, and the First Modern Monopoly {#sec-1-08}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act I — The World Before California · 1700–1848
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does infrastructure become sovereignty?

**The answer.** By owning the preconditions rather than the goods. Steam, rail,
and coal produced the first firms with structural control over the terms on
which economic life was possible — and the East India Company showed that a
corporation could govern a territory outright. Meanwhile the age's revolutions
established that natural rights language and property claims could be made to
say the same thing.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, arriving in
its modern form, with the corporation as the vehicle. Whoever owns the rails
sets the prices; whoever owns the ports owns the trade. The chapter's job is to
make the reader recognise the Central Pacific before meeting it.

**The key fact.** The East India Company was the first corporation to govern a
territory — raising taxes, keeping an army, and administering law over tens of
millions of people. Corporate sovereignty is not a twenty-first-century anxiety;
it is a documented eighteenth-century fact.

**The human anchor.** John Jacob Astor, dying in March 1848 as the richest man
in America, having made his fortune in furs and kept it in Manhattan real
estate. Nine days later a carpenter finds gold in a millrace in Coloma. The old
model of American fortune ends in the same season the new one begins.

**Excluded voices.** The enslaved people whose labour financed the industrial
economy's inputs, the Bengali weavers ruined by Company policy, and the
property-less majority in whose name the Atlantic revolutions were fought and to
whom the resulting franchise was not extended.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that infrastructure ownership is a form of
sovereignty by showing a chartered company governing a subcontinent, and that
the American revolution was substantially a property settlement by showing who
held the franchise afterwards.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

John Jacob Astor died in March 1848, the richest man in America, having made his
fortune in furs and kept it in Manhattan real estate. Nine days earlier a
carpenter had found gold in a millrace at Coloma, California. Neither event knew
about the other. The old model of American fortune ended in the same season the
new one began, and Act I ends on that seam.

Before it gets there the chapter does two jobs. The first is the Enlightenment,
whose effect was not to topple kings but to make their authority intellectually
indefensible, which is slower and more dangerous. The American Revolution
succeeded as a property settlement conducted in natural-rights language, and the
propertied class won it — a claim the chapter supports with the franchise
records rather than by assertion, after giving the idealist reading its
strongest form. The French Revolution was more honest about being a transfer of
sovereignty and therefore more violent. Napoleon resolved the contradiction by
colonising republican vocabulary while concentrating imperial power, which is
precisely what Augustus did, and the pattern is holding.

The second job is monopoly in its modern form. Steam, rail, and coal produced
firms with structural control over the preconditions of economic life rather
than mere advantages within it. Whoever owns the rails sets the prices; whoever
controls the ports controls the trade. And the East India Company demonstrated
the end state: a chartered corporation with an army, a tax base, and
administrative authority over tens of millions of people. Corporate sovereignty
is not a twenty-first-century anxiety. It is a documented eighteenth-century
fact.

The cost is in the inputs. Enslaved labour financed much of the industrial
economy's raw material, and Company policy ruined the Bengali weaving industry
that had been the world's largest.

The pattern is now established across three thousand years and four continents.
Act II runs it again from the beginning, in one place, within a single lifetime,
and on the record.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does infrastructure become sovereignty?
:::

John Jacob Astor died in New York on 29 March 1848, the richest man in America.
He had made the fortune in furs and moved it into Manhattan real estate, on the
correct assessment that the island would fill up and that rent was more reliable
than beaver.

Nine days earlier and three thousand miles west, at a sawmill on the American
River, a carpenter named James Marshall had picked flakes of metal out of a
tailrace. Neither man knew about the other. Astor died without hearing of the
discovery, and Marshall spent the rest of his life failing to profit from it.

The old model of the American fortune ended in the same season the new one
began. Act I ends on that seam, and everything before it in this chapter is the
explanation of why the new one would look the way it did.

## The Enlightenment's actual effect

The eighteenth century did not topple kings by argument. It did something slower
and more corrosive: it made their authority intellectually indefensible, and
left the institutions standing while the justification eroded underneath them.

Once sovereignty is understood as deriving from the consent of the governed
rather than from God, every existing arrangement becomes a question rather than
a fact. This does not immediately change who holds power. It changes what
defenders of power have to say, and once they are obliged to argue on the new
terms they have already conceded the important point.

The American Revolution is the case this book cares about, and the honest
reading requires giving the idealist version its full weight first. The
Declaration asserts a general principle in universal language, the
constitutional settlement that followed was a genuine achievement in
institutional design, and a great many people who fought believed what they
said. None of that is decoration.

It is also true that the revolution was, in substantial part, a dispute about
property conducted in the vocabulary of natural rights, and that the propertied
won it. The grievances that mobilised the colonial elite were about taxation,
western land claims, and commercial regulation. The settlement that followed
extended the franchise to property-holding white men and to nobody else. Slavery
was preserved and constitutionally accommodated. The western territories whose
disposition had been a central grievance were opened to speculation, and the men
who had led the revolution were frequently the speculators.

The French Revolution was more honest about being a transfer of sovereignty and
was therefore more violent, because a transfer of sovereignty has losers who
understand themselves as such. And Napoleon resolved the contradiction the way
it had been resolved before: he retained the republican vocabulary, the codes,
the plebiscites, and the language of the nation, while concentrating imperial
power in one person.

Augustus did this in 27 BCE. Chapter 3 described it. The pattern is holding.

## Infrastructure becomes sovereignty

The economic transformation running alongside all of this produced something
genuinely new, and this book's whole argument depends on getting the novelty
right.

Merchants had always sought advantage. What steam, coal, and rail produced was
different in kind: firms with structural control over the preconditions of
economic activity rather than an edge within it. A textile manufacturer with a
better machine has an advantage that competitors can copy. A railway company
that owns the only line between a mining district and a port has something else
entirely. It does not need to make anything. It sets the terms on which everyone
else's making reaches a market.

Whoever owns the rails sets the prices. Whoever controls the ports controls the
trade. The distinguishing feature of this kind of position is that it does not
have to compete, because the competition would have to reproduce the
infrastructure first, and the infrastructure is expensive, slow, and frequently
protected by a charter.

Britain built the first version of it and exported the model, and the capital
requirements pushed the corporate form into general use: the joint-stock company
with limited liability, which allows an enterprise to outlive its founders and
to raise money from people with no involvement in running it. This is the
vehicle that carries everything in the rest of this book.

## The company that governed a subcontinent

The end state was already visible, and it had been for decades.

The English East India Company was chartered in 1600 as a trading concern. By
the middle of the eighteenth century it maintained its own armies, and after the
grant of the *diwani* in 1765 it held the right to collect the land revenue of
Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa — which is to say that a joint-stock company with
shareholders in London was the tax authority for tens of millions of people. It
administered justice, waged war, negotiated treaties, and set trade policy in
its own interest.

The results were what one would expect from an arrangement in which the taxing
authority and the principal trader were the same body. The Bengal famine of 1770
killed a large fraction of the population of the region while revenue collection
continued. The Bengali textile industry, which had been the largest in the
world, was systematically disadvantaged in favour of British manufactures.

Parliament spent the following decades trying to bring the Company under
control, which is itself informative: the state that had chartered the
corporation discovered that recovering authority from it was difficult,
expensive, and protracted. Corporate sovereignty is not a twenty-first-century
anxiety. It is a documented eighteenth-century fact, and everyone in the
nineteenth century knew it.

## The American variation

Britain built its railways with private capital and fought about the resulting
monopolies afterwards. The United States, with more territory than capital and a
government that owned enormous quantities of land it could not otherwise
monetise, invented a different instrument.

The land grant worked like this. A company undertaking to build a line through
unsettled territory received, in addition to the right of way, alternate
sections of public land along the route — typically in a checkerboard pattern
extending some miles on either side. The company could sell the land to finance
construction, and the land became valuable precisely because the railway was
being built across it. The government retained the intervening sections, which
also appreciated, and this was the official justification: the public would
recover its contribution through the increased value of what it kept.

The Illinois Central received the first major federal grant of this kind in
1850, and the model was then applied on a far larger scale to the
transcontinental lines. Its elegance is that it appears to cost the treasury
nothing. No appropriation is required. No tax is raised. Land that was
generating no revenue is exchanged for infrastructure, and the transaction shows
up in no budget as an expenditure.

It is nonetheless a subsidy, and an enormous one, and it has two features worth
carrying into Act II. The land was public, which is to say it had been taken
from somebody, and the taking is not recorded in the grant. And the resulting
asset was private and permanent — a corporation ended up owning a substantial
fraction of the American West outright, with no obligation to the public beyond
running trains.

Every element of the machine that will make four Sacramento merchants into the
wealthiest men on the Pacific coast is now in existence. What is missing is a
decision about where the line should run, and that decision will be made in
Washington by subtraction.

## The seam

Which returns us to Astor.

His fortune began in the fur trade, which is extraction — take a resource from a
territory, using the labour and knowledge of people who live there, and sell it
somewhere else. He then converted the proceeds into Manhattan land and collected
rent on the growth of a city he had no part in building. Extraction converted
into rent: the oldest American pattern, and the one about to be run again on a
much larger scale on the other side of the continent.

Because on 24 January 1848 James Marshall found gold in the tailrace at Coloma,
and nine days later, on 2 February, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred
California to the United States. The negotiators in Mexico did not know. Nobody
in Washington knew. For several weeks the most valuable real estate on the
continent changed hands at a price set in ignorance.

The pattern this act has traced — chokepoint control, public authority converted
to private benefit, institutions reproducing the class that endows them — took
three thousand years to establish across four continents and a dozen
civilisations. In California it runs again from the beginning, in one place,
compressed into a single lifetime, and this time the documents survive.

*Cardinal* is the proof. The last movement of this book is how the title
moved.
